processing: A fine baked green (hong qing): tender leaf is heated to stop oxidation, rolled into tight downy strips, and finished by baking rather than pan-firing.
harvest_season: Exact dates are not fixed in the records. Like other fine Mengding greens, it is a spring tea, with early pickings most prized.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine and even strips, fresh tender green with plenty of visible down.
appearance_wet: Even, tender green leaves and buds.
taste_profile: A clean, high, fresh aroma leads to a fairly full and brisk cup, with enough strength to stay pleasant through a few steeps.

brewing.notes: The down clouds the first cup a little, which is normal. Pour water gently down the side of the vessel.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring tea and best drunk within about a year, like most Chinese greens. Early spring lots command more. It is listed alongside Mengding Ganlu, Shihua and Huangya, so make sure you know which Mengding style you are buying.
description:
Meng Ding Mao Feng is a downy baked green tea from Mengding Mountain in Ya'an, one of the Mengshan family alongside Ganlu, Shihua and Huangya. Where Ganlu is the famous curled tea, Mao Feng is the simpler straight strip that shows off its fine hairs.

Mao feng literally describes the look, downy tips, and is broadly used for fine baked greens. Tender leaf is rolled tight and dried by baking, which keeps the down and gives a clean, lifted aroma.

The cup is pale yellow with a fresh smell and a fuller, brisker taste than the delicate look suggests. Brew at about 80°C, and do not worry if the first infusion is slightly hazy; that is the fine hair, not a fault.

The term mao feng turns up across China, so Mengding on the label matters, and so does the picking date. Good leaf is even, tight and green with lots of down, rather than dull or broken.
history:
Tea from Mengding has a long reputation, summed up in the saying about Yangtze water and Mengshan tea. Local accounts claim the mountain's tea was admired under flowery names as far back as the Eastern Han, and that it was sent to court as tribute from the Tang through to the Qing. Those accounts concern the tea of the mountain generally; how far they apply to this particular style is unclear.

Mao Feng itself is best understood as one of the mountain's named present-day styles. The name is registered as a certification trademark for a geographical indication.
